docs.title: Pyramids QGIS
docs.text:
A QGIS plugin that exposes the pyramids GIS toolkit (pyramids-core) as a QGIS Processing provider. The algorithms appear in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids, so they work in the toolbox, the graphical modeler, batch mode, the Python processing.run(...) API, and the qgis_process command line — the same as any native QGIS algorithm.

Status: experimental

First release ships file-in / file-out raster, conversion, mesh, and Earth-observation algorithms. The raster and conversion algorithms mirror the pyramids command-line interface; the mesh and EO algorithms call their backing libraries directly (see How it works below). The plugin is marked experimental=True in its metadata.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The plugin is a thin adapter that carries no GIS logic of its own. There are two ways an algorithm reaches pyramids:

  • CLI-backed (most raster + all conversion algorithms). Each algorithm translates its QGIS parameters into a pyramids <command> ... argument list and calls the pyramids CLI in-process (pyramids.cli.main). The CLI maps 1:1 onto library calls and is pyramids' stable, documented contract, so the plugin never re-implements raster logic and never drifts from the library.
  • Library-direct (mesh + Earth-observation algorithms). Those backing packages have no CLI, so the algorithm imports and calls the library directly — MeshDataset for mesh, pyramids_eo for EO.

Work is passed by file path, never by in-memory GDAL objects: QGIS hands pyramids an input path, pyramids writes an output file, and QGIS loads it as a new layer. This deliberately avoids sharing live gdal.Dataset handles across two GDAL builds in one process.

docs.title: The dependency tiers
docs.text:
Three backing packages, three tiers of strictness, all checked in the plugin's dependencies.py:

Package Requirement Needed for pyramids-core always required (hard error if missing) every algorithm pyramids-eo required for the EO algorithms only (hard error) contrast stretch, tasseled cap pyramids-mesh optional even for the mesh algorithms (soft warning) mesh formats other than UGRID NetCDF

The critical constraint is that pyramids-core must be importable from the interpreter QGIS runs and bound to QGIS's own GDAL — not a platform wheel that vendors its own GDAL. See Installation.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Installation — install the backing libraries into QGIS's Python and deploy the plugin into a QGIS profile.
  • End-to-end testing — the by-hand validation guide: what to run, what to watch for, and when the plugin is done.
  • Algorithms — the full list of algorithms the provider ships, grouped by raster, conversion, mesh, and Earth observation.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
Every algorithm is file-in / file-out — work is passed by file path, never by a live in-memory gdal.Dataset handle. They appear in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids, split into the groups below.

Each algorithm's own help text (the right-hand pane of its dialog) is the authoritative description of its parameters; this page is the map of what exists and what it maps to in pyramids.

The Processing id column is what you pass to processing.run(...), e.g. processing.run("pyramids:raster_align", {...}). Most algorithms are CLI-backed: the plugin builds a pyramids <command> ... argument list and runs it in-process, so the command column is the pyramids CLI invocation behind the algorithm. The Mesh and Earth-observation groups call their library directly instead.

There are 92 algorithms across 10 groups:

Group Algorithms Raster 33 Vector 36 Collection 6 NetCDF 4 Mesh 2 Earth Observation 2 Fetch 5 STAC 1 Process 2 Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF 1

docs.text:
Operations over a stack of rasters (a datacube / time series) rather than a single file.

docs.title: NetCDF
docs.text:
Reach into a NetCDF file: crop it, pull a variable or group out, or select a time step.

Algorithm Processing id pyramids command Crop NetCDF (by bounding box) pyramids:nc_crop nc crop Extract NetCDF group pyramids:nc_get_group nc get-group Extract NetCDF variable to raster pyramids:nc_extract nc extract Select NetCDF time step pyramids:nc_sel nc sel

docs.title: Mesh
docs.text:
These wrap pyramids' MeshDataset directly rather than the CLI, since pyramids-mesh has no CLI. UGRID NetCDF is built in; other formats (2DM, Selafin, DFSU, XMDF, PLY, …) need pyramids-mesh installed.

Algorithm Processing id pyramids API Convert mesh format pyramids:mesh_convert MeshDataset.read_file / to_file Mesh to vector pyramids:mesh_to_vector MeshDataset.to_geodataframe → FeatureCollection.to_file

docs.title: Earth Observation
docs.text:
These wrap pyramids-eo directly, since it has no CLI. They require pyramids-eo to be installed — it is a hard requirement for this group only.

Algorithm Processing id pyramids API Contrast stretch (EO) pyramids:eo_stretch pyramids_eo.enhance.stretch Tasseled cap transform pyramids:tasseled_cap pyramids_eo.spectral.tasseled_cap

docs.text:

docs.title: Process
docs.text:
Drive pyramids' own processing registry: apply a single tool, or run a whole pipeline.

Algorithm Processing id pyramids command Apply processing tool pyramids:process_apply process apply Run processing pipeline pyramids:process_run process run

docs.title: Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
docs.text:
A single algorithm, in its own toolbox group.

Algorithm Processing id pyramids command Create Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF pyramids:cog_create raster cog create

docs.title: Example data
docs.text: The repo ships a tiny, self-contained dataset under examples/data/ to try the algorithms on: a 32×32 EPSG:4326 DEM (dem.tif) and a polygon AOI (aoi.geojson). See examples/README.md for copy-paste processing.run(...) snippets.

docs.title: Not covered yet
docs.text:
• Terrain derivatives — slope, aspect and hillshade have no algorithm yet.
  • An interactive dock widget for COG preview / STAC browsing. The plugin is deliberately Processing-only today: it registers a provider and adds no toolbar, menu or panel.

docs.title: Continuous integration & delivery
docs.text:
This repository is driven by seven GitHub Actions workflows. This page explains what triggers each one and where its output goes — nothing (a pass/fail gate), a run-scoped workflow artifact, a GitHub Release asset, the gh-pages site, or the official plugins.qgis.org repository.

The plugin is not published to PyPI — pyramids-qgis ships as a QGIS plugin zip. "Publishing" therefore means attaching that zip (and a custom-repository plugins.xml) to a GitHub Release and uploading it to plugins.qgis.org, not pushing a wheel to PyPI. (The Wheel - Build & Test workflow does build a wheel, but only to test the import surface — that wheel is never released.)

docs.title: Workflows at a glance
docs.text: Workflow File Triggers Output / uploaded to CI lint.yml push → main, pull_request none — gate only (ruff, byte-compile 3.11/3.12/3.13, gitleaks) Tests tests.yml push → main, pull_request none — gate only (pytest against real QGIS, matrix dev + qt5) Wheel - Build & Test pure-wheel-test.yml push → main, pull_request, workflow_dispatch run-scoped artifact (the built wheel, passed build → test across ubuntu/macos/windows) pip-audit pip-audit.yml pull_request, schedule (Mon 06:00 UTC), workflow_dispatch none — gate only (dependency audit in the run log) Deploy MkDocs github-pages-mkdocs.yml push → main, pull_request, release published, workflow_run ← github-release PR → run-scoped artifact (site-pr-<n> preview); main/release → the gh-pages site github-release github-release.yml workflow_dispatch (release-branch, increment, draft) a GitHub Release + git tag (via cz bump → action-gh-release) publish publish.yml workflow_run ← github-release, workflow_dispatch (branch) workflow_run → GitHub Release assets (+ plugins.qgis.org); dispatch → run-scoped artifacts

docs.title: The five destinations
docs.text:
• Gate only — the workflow just passes or fails a commit/PR; it uploads nothing durable.
  • Run-scoped workflow artifact — a file attached to that one Actions run (download it from the run page; it expires). Used for the built wheel and the per-PR docs preview, and by publish's manual path.
  • GitHub Release asset — a file permanently attached to a Release (.../releases/download/<tag>/...). The plugin zip and plugins.xml live here.
  • gh-pages site — the rendered documentation, committed to the gh-pages branch by mike and served by GitHub Pages.
  • plugins.qgis.org — the official QGIS plugin repository (the real "publish"). Inert until the QGIS_TOKEN secret is set.

docs.title: How triggers map to workflows
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    PR([Pull request]) --> CI[CI: lint.yml]
    PR --> TST[Tests: tests.yml]
    PR --> WHL[Wheel: pure-wheel-test.yml]
    PR --> AUD[pip-audit.yml]
    PR --> DOCpr[Deploy MkDocs: build-strict]

    PUSH([Push to main]) --> CI
    PUSH --> TST
    PUSH --> WHL
    PUSH --> DOCmain[Deploy MkDocs: deploy-main]

    CRON([Schedule: Mon 06:00 UTC]) --> AUD
    MANW([Manual dispatch]) --> WHL
    MANW --> AUD
    MANP([Manual dispatch + branch]) --> PUBd[publish.yml: artifact path]

    REL([Manual dispatch: github-release.yml]) --> RELj[cz bump → tag → GitHub Release]
    RELj -. workflow_run .-> PUBr[publish.yml: release path]
    RELj -. workflow_run .-> DOCrel[Deploy MkDocs: deploy-release]

    DOCpr --> A1[/site-pr-n artifact/]
    DOCmain --> GP[(gh-pages site)]
    DOCrel --> GP
    WHL --> A2[/wheel artifact/]
    PUBd --> A3[/zip + plugins.xml artifacts/]
    PUBr --> RA[(Release assets: zip + plugins.xml)]
    PUBr --> QG[(plugins.qgis.org)]

docs.title: Everyday CI — pull request and push to main
docs.text:
Every PR runs four gates — CI, Tests, pip-audit, Wheel — plus a strict docs build. A push to main runs the same set except pip-audit, which is pull-request- and schedule-only. None of them publish; the docs build only uploads a preview on PRs.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Gates["Gates — pass/fail only"]
        L["CI (lint.yml)<br/>ruff · byte-compile 3.11/3.12/3.13 · gitleaks"]
        T["Tests (tests.yml)<br/>pytest vs real QGIS · dev + qt5"]
        A["pip-audit.yml<br/>(PRs + weekly)"]
    end
    EV([PR or push to main]) --> L
    EV --> T
    EV -->|PR only| A
    EV --> W["Wheel (pure-wheel-test.yml)"]
    EV --> D["Deploy MkDocs: build-strict<br/>(warnings = errors)"]

    W -->|build-wheel| WA[/wheel artifact/]
    WA -->|download| WT["test-wheel<br/>ubuntu · macos · windows"]
    D -->|pull_request only| PRA[/site-pr-n preview artifact/]
    D -->|push to main| DM[deploy-main ⟶ gh-pages]

The wheel artifact is internal to the run: build-wheel uploads it and test-wheel downloads it to install and test on all three OSes. It is not a release.

docs.title: The release pipeline
docs.text:
A release is started by hand by dispatching github-release.yml. That job bumps the version with commitizen, pushes the bump commit and the bare tag (0.1.1, not v0.1.1), and creates the GitHub Release. Because a Release created with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN cannot trigger another workflow directly, two workflows listen for github-release to complete via workflow_run:

flowchart TD
    M([Maintainer dispatches github-release.yml<br/>inputs: release-branch, increment, draft]) --> CZ["cz bump:<br/>version + CHANGELOG + bare tag"]
    CZ --> PUSH[push commit + tag to the release branch]
    PUSH --> GR[(Create GitHub Release)]

    GR -. "workflow_run: github-release completed" .-> PUB
    GR -. "workflow_run: github-release completed" .-> DR[Deploy MkDocs: deploy-release]

    subgraph PUB["publish.yml — release path"]
        PC["Checkout the TIP of the release branch<br/>= the commitizen-bumped version"] --> PB["qgis-plugin-ci release --create-plugin-repo"]
        PB --> PR[("Release assets:<br/>the plugin zip + plugins.xml")]
        PB --> PQ[("plugins.qgis.org<br/>inert without OSGEO secrets")]
    end

    DR --> GP[("gh-pages: versioned docs via mike")]

Checking out the tip of the release branch (not the triggering commit) is essential: github-release pushes the version-bump commit after the workflow_run SHA is captured, so only the branch tip carries the bumped metadata.txt version. The build then checks out that version's tag before packaging, so the Release asset is exactly the tagged commit even if another commit lands on the branch meanwhile.

Caveat — a draft release gets no plugin assets. The release path only uploads when a published Release exists for the tag (the gate queries /releases/tags/<tag>, which does not return drafts). If github-release is dispatched with draft: true, publish.yml finds no published Release, emits a ::warning::, and the job still goes green with nothing uploaded. Publishing the draft later fires a release event, which publish.yml does not listen for — so publish the Release (non-draft) as part of cutting it, or re-cut the version.

docs.title: publish.yml — two paths, chosen by trigger
docs.text:
publish.yml builds the same plugin zip + plugins.xml either way, but where they go depends on how it was triggered:

flowchart TD
    START([publish.yml])

    START --> R{Trigger?}

    R -->|workflow_run<br/>after github-release| RR[Checkout release branch TIP]
    RR --> RB["qgis-plugin-ci release --create-plugin-repo"]
    RB --> RREL[(Upload zip + plugins.xml<br/>to the GitHub Release)]
    RB --> RQ[(Upload to plugins.qgis.org<br/>if OSGEO secrets set)]

    R -->|workflow_dispatch<br/>input: branch| DD[Checkout the given branch TIP]
    DD --> DB["qgis-plugin-ci package --plugin-repo-url"]
    DB --> DART[/"Upload zip + plugins.xml<br/>as workflow artifacts<br/>(name: pyramids_qgis-VERSION)"/]
  • workflow_run → Release. The real publish. qgis-plugin-ci release needs a published Release to attach to, which github-release has just created, and --create-plugin-repo also generates and uploads plugins.xml.
  • workflow_dispatch → artifacts only. A safe, throwaway build of any branch for inspection. It uses qgis-plugin-ci package (which needs no Release) and uploads the results as run-scoped artifacts — it never touches a Release. Build from main by hand here without risk of attaching the wrong source to a release.

Why the split exists: when both triggers uploaded to the Release and the manual path checked out main instead of the tag, a hand-run build once attached main's source (including post-tag commits) to an already-cut release. Routing workflow_dispatch to artifacts removes that hazard entirely.

docs.title: Documentation (MkDocs) deployment
docs.text:
github-pages-mkdocs.yml always runs a strict (warnings-as-errors) build as a gate, then publishes only for main and releases. Pull requests build the site and upload a preview artifact but never publish it.

flowchart TD
    EV{Trigger}
    EV -->|pull_request| BS[build-strict gate]
    BS --> PRA[/site-pr-n preview artifact<br/>reviewers download it/]

    EV -->|push to main| DMg[build-strict ⟶ deploy-main]
    DMg --> GPm[(gh-pages: latest docs via mike)]

    EV -->|release published<br/>OR workflow_run ← github-release| DRg[build-strict ⟶ deploy-release]
    DRg --> GPr[(gh-pages: versioned docs via mike)]

mike publishes by committing the rendered site to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves (Settings → Pages → Source = gh-pages). PR previews are deliberately not published — each one would otherwise commit a full site onto the shared gh-pages branch.

deploy-release's release: published trigger fires only for a manually published Release. A Release created by github-release.yml with the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN does not emit a release event, so in the automated release flow deploy-release runs via the workflow_run path only.

docs.text: Secret Used by Effect when unset GITHUB_TOKEN (built-in) all always present ACTIONS_DEPLOY_TOKEN Deploy MkDocs (deploy jobs) docs cannot push to gh-pages QGIS_TOKEN publish.yml (release path) plugins.qgis.org upload is skipped; the Release assets still publish

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Pyramids QGIS is on the official QGIS plugin repository, so you install it from inside QGIS:

  1. Plugins → Manage and Install Plugins…
  2. On the Settings tab, tick "Show also experimental plugins" (the plugin is published as experimental, so it is hidden otherwise).
  3. On the All tab, search for Pyramids QGIS and click Install Plugin.

The algorithms then appear in the Processing Toolbox under Pyramids — see the Usage tutorial.

The plugin installs pyramids-core for you

The algorithms call the pyramids library, so pyramids-core 0.81.0 or newer must be importable from the Python QGIS runs. The plugin checks on load and offers to install — or upgrade — it into QGIS's own interpreter: choose Yes, let it finish (QGIS is unresponsive for a few minutes, with no progress bar), then restart QGIS. Not now asks again next start; Don't ask again suppresses the offer.

To do it yourself instead — or if the install fails — run pip install 'pyramids-core>=0.81.0' against the Python QGIS runs, then restart QGIS. On a conda/OSGeo4W QGIS the conda-forge package is named pyramids (the PyPI distribution is pyramids-core; both import as pyramids). The Earth-observation algorithms additionally need pyramids-eo.

docs.title: End-to-end testing
docs.text:
The unit / integration suite runs against real PyQGIS in CI and exercises every algorithm's initAlgorithm / parameter construction. What it does not cover is running an algorithm end-to-end (processAlgorithm) in a real QGIS session on real data, nor the GUI / dialog behaviour. That still has to be done by hand, and it is the gate before a non-experimental release.

This page is that by-hand validation guide. Install the plugin first — see Installation.

docs.title: What to run — cover both wiring paths and every group
docs.text:
88 of the 92 algorithms call the pyramids CLI in-process; only the Mesh and Earth-observation groups call their library directly. Run at least one of each path, and at least one per group:

  • [ ] Raster (CLI path): Reproject (warp) a GeoTIFF to another CRS; confirm the output layer loads and looks right.
  • [ ] Raster: Clip (by mask and by extent), Merge, Raster calculator (e.g. NDVI over two inputs), Assign CRS / NoData — and the format-conversion ones that also live in this group: Rasterize a vector, Polygonize a raster (GeoJSON output), Convert format.
  • [ ] Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF: Create COG, and confirm the result validates as a COG.
  • [ ] Vector: one of each kind — a geometry op (buffer / simplify), an overlay (clip or intersection), and a tessellation (fishnet or Voronoi).
  • [ ] Collection: one whole-stack operation (align or reduce over time) on a small stack.
  • [ ] NetCDF: extract a variable to raster, and select a time step.
  • [ ] Fetch: pull a small window from a public WMS or WFS (needs network).
  • [ ] STAC: download an asset from a public catalogue (needs network).
  • [ ] Process: apply a processing tool, and run a short pipeline.
  • [ ] Mesh (library path): Convert a .2dm / Selafin mesh to UGRID NetCDF, and Mesh → vector (needs pyramids-mesh).
  • [ ] EO (library path): Contrast stretch, and Tasseled cap on a Landsat reflectance stack (needs pyramids-eo).

docs.title: What to watch for — things CI cannot catch
docs.text:
• [ ] PyQGIS parameter wiring — each algorithm's parameterAs* calls, enum / attribute names, and the dialog rendering. (initAlgorithm / parameter construction is covered automatically by the real-QGIS integration tests; the dialog rendering and actual execution are not.)
  • [ ] Forced-GeoJSON output — the provider pins vector outputs to .geojson; confirm Polygonize / Mesh → vector produce loadable GeoJSON and the extension matches the content.
  • [ ] Dependency guards — with pyramids-mesh / pyramids-eo absent, the mesh / EO algorithms should raise a clear "install ..." message; the vendored-GDAL warning should appear only for a vendored build.
  • [ ] The pyramids-core install offer — no automated test can reach it. With pyramids-core absent (and again with a version below 0.81.0), starting QGIS should show the offer after the main window appears, not block startup. Check all three buttons: Yes installs into the interpreter the dialog names and then asks for a restart; Not now re-offers on the next start; Don't ask again does not. A failed install should show the manual pip command.
  • [ ] Error surfacing — a bad CRS / missing file should come back as a clean QgsProcessingException in the Processing log, not a raw traceback.
  • [ ] Headless (qgis_process) — enable it in that profile first (qgis_process plugins enable pyramids_qgis), or it reports no algorithms for the ordinary reason that it is switched off. Then qgis_process plugins must list * pyramids_qgis (the * means it loaded as a Processing provider) and qgis_process list must show the pyramids: algorithms; then run one to an output file. This path is separate from the GUI: QGIS starts the plugin through initProcessing rather than initGui, so a missing hook shows up here and nowhere else.
  • [ ] Qt5 / Qt6 — ideally smoke-test on a QGIS 3.x (Qt5) and a 4.x (Qt6) build, since the plugin uses the qgis.PyQt shim.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• [ ] At least one algorithm per group runs successfully on real data and loads a correct output layer.
  • [ ] The dependency-guard and error-surfacing behaviour is confirmed.
  • [ ] Any bugs found are filed as their own issues (and fixed) before flipping experimental=False in metadata.txt.

docs.title: Usage tutorial
docs.text:
Pyramids QGIS is a Processing provider — it adds algorithms, not a toolbar or a menu. Everything you run lives in the Processing Toolbox, so the algorithms work the same way as any native QGIS tool: in the toolbox, the graphical modeler, batch mode, the Python processing.run(...) API, and the qgis_process command line.

This page walks through finding the algorithms and running a couple of them end to end. For the full catalogue of what each algorithm does, see the Algorithms reference.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Install the plugin from the QGIS Plugin Manager — see Installation. The plugin checks for its pyramids-core dependency when it loads and offers to install it into QGIS's Python if it is missing or older than 0.81.0, so there is usually nothing else to set up.

docs.title: 1. Find the algorithms
docs.text:
Open the toolbox with Processing → Toolbox (or Ctrl+Alt+T), then expand the Pyramids provider. The algorithms are grouped by theme:

  • Raster — reproject (warp), clip, raster calculator, merge, edit info, convert format, rasterize, polygonize, and much more (the largest group).
  • Vector — geometry operations (buffer, simplify, make valid, rotate, scale), overlays (clip, union, intersection, difference, dissolve, spatial joins) and tessellation (fishnet, Voronoi, Delaunay, quadtree, H3).
  • Collection — whole-stack raster operations: align to a reference grid, crop, merge (mosaic), reduce over time, reproject, resample.
  • NetCDF — crop by bounding box, extract a variable to raster, extract a group, select a time step.
  • Mesh — convert mesh format, mesh to vector.
  • Earth Observation — contrast stretch, tasseled cap transform.
  • Fetch — pull a window or features from OGC services: WMS, WMTS, WFS, WCS, OGC API Coverages.
  • STAC — download STAC assets.
  • Process — apply a processing tool, run a processing pipeline.
  • Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF — create a COG.

Every algorithm ships its own help text, shown in the right-hand pane of its dialog — that is the authoritative description of its parameters. The Algorithms reference lists all 92 algorithms by group, with the Processing id and the pyramids command behind each one.

If the Pyramids group is not there, the plugin did not load — recheck the install and that pyramids-core imports in the QGIS Python console (import pyramids).

docs.title: 2. Worked example — reproject a raster (warp)
docs.text:
1. Load a raster into QGIS (Layer → Add Layer → Add Raster Layer…), or just have the file path handy.
  2. In the toolbox, open Pyramids → Raster → Reproject raster (warp).
  3. Fill the dialog:
    • Input raster — your layer (or … → choose a file).
    • Target CRS — the CRS to reproject into, e.g. EPSG:3857.
    • Resampling method — defaults to nearest neighbor; pick bilinear or cubic for continuous data.
    • Reprojected raster — an output path (or leave it to a temporary file).
  4. Click Run. The algorithm writes the output file and loads it as a new layer.

That is the whole pattern: pick an input, set parameters, give an output path, Run. Every Pyramids algorithm follows it.

docs.title: 3. Worked example — clip a raster
docs.text:
Pyramids → Raster → Clip raster (by mask or extent) crops a raster two ways:

  • By mask — set Mask layer (polygons) to a polygon layer; the raster is cut to those polygons.
  • By extent — leave the mask empty and set Clip extent (drag on the canvas, or type a bounding box). The extent is read in the input raster's CRS.

If you give both, the mask wins. Set an output path and Run.

docs.title: 4. The file-in / file-out model
docs.text:
Pyramids algorithms are file-in / file-out: QGIS hands pyramids an input path, pyramids writes an output file, and QGIS loads that file as a new layer. They never operate on a live in-memory raster.

The practical consequence: a scratch / memory layer must be saved to disk first. If an input only exists in memory (for example the output of another tool kept as a temporary layer), export it (right-click → Export → Save As…) and point the algorithm at the saved file.

docs.title: 5. Beyond the toolbox
docs.text:
Because these are standard Processing algorithms, they also run:

  • Batch — right-click an algorithm → Execute as Batch Process… to run it over many inputs at once.
  • Graphical Modeler — drag a Pyramids algorithm into a model to chain it with other steps.

  • qgis_process — run an algorithm from a shell, with no QGIS window open at all:

    qgis_process plugins enable pyramids_qgis    # once per profile
qgis_process plugins                         # '* pyramids_qgis' means it loaded
qgis_process list                            # every algorithm, including the pyramids: ones
qgis_process run pyramids:warp -- INPUT=dem.tif CRS=EPSG:3857 OUTPUT=out.tif

    The plugin must be enabled in the profile qgis_process uses; pyramids-core still has to be installed in that QGIS's Python, and the install offer never appears here because there is no GUI to show it in. - Python console — call it by its provider-qualified id, pyramids:<name>:

    import processing

# Reproject to Web Mercator with bilinear resampling.
processing.run(
    "pyramids:warp",
    {
        "INPUT": "C:/data/dem.tif",  # a file path or a loaded layer
        "CRS": "EPSG:3857",
        "RESAMPLING": 1,  # index into [nearest, bilinear, cubic, cubic_spline, lanczos, average, mode]
        "OUTPUT": "C:/data/dem_3857.tif",
    },
)

# Clip to a polygon mask.
processing.run(
    "pyramids:clip",
    {
        "INPUT": "C:/data/dem.tif",
        "MASK": "C:/data/aoi.gpkg",
        "OUTPUT": "C:/data/dem_clipped.tif",
    },
)

    The parameter keys are the UPPERCASE names shown here (INPUT, CRS, OUTPUT, …); RESAMPLING is an enum, so it takes the integer index of the method.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "pyramids is not importable" / every algorithm fails immediately — pyramids-core is missing from the QGIS Python, or is older than 0.81.0. The plugin offers to install it on load; if you dismissed that with Don't ask again, install it yourself (pip install 'pyramids-core>=0.81.0') and restart QGIS. See Installation.
  • The Earth-observation algorithms fail with a dependency error — those need pyramids-eo (a hard requirement for the EO group only). Install it into the QGIS interpreter.
  • A non-UGRID mesh format fails — mesh formats beyond UGRID NetCDF need the optional pyramids-mesh; the plugin warns rather than hard-fails when it is absent.
  • A warning that the input "is not a local file" — the plugin warns rather than refusing, then the run fails downstream. Usually it means the input is an in-memory/scratch or database layer: save it to a file first (see The file-in / file-out model). Remote and /vsi… paths are fine and warn harmlessly.

docs.title: Change-log
docs.text:
The project's change-log is generated by commitizen from the Conventional Commit history on each release (cz bump, run by the github-release workflow) and written to CHANGELOG.md at the repo root. It is not edited by hand — any manual change is overwritten on the next release.

The first tagged release populates it from the commit history to date. Until then, see the commit history and the Releases page on GitHub.
